front: What are the four ways energy can be transferred between stores?
answer: Mechanically (by a force) / Electrically (by a current) / By heating / By radiation (light or sound)
title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power

front: Why does an object's kinetic energy quadruple when its speed doubles?
answer: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 2 squared, which is 4.
title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power

front: Why does a spring's elastic potential energy quadruple when its extension doubles?
answer: Elastic potential energy depends on extension squared, so doubling the extension multiplies the energy by 2 squared, which is 4.
title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power

front: Plant cells have three structures that animal cells lack. What are they?
answer: Chloroplasts / Permanent vacuole / Cell wall
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: What are the four prefixes for units smaller than a metre, from largest to smallest, with their powers of ten?
answer: centi (10⁻²) / milli (10⁻³) / micro (10⁻⁶) / nano (10⁻⁹)
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Why does the cell wall stop a plant cell bursting when water enters it by osmosis?
answer: The cellulose cell wall is strong and rigid, so it resists the extra pressure and holds the cell together.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: Why do muscle cells contain more mitochondria than many other cells?
answer: Mitochondria are where aerobic respiration happens, and muscle cells need extra energy from respiration to contract.
title: Cell Structure and Microscopy

front: What are the four techniques used to separate mixtures?
answer: Filtration / Simple distillation / Fractional distillation / Chromatography
title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

front: What are the relative charges of the three subatomic particles?
answer: Proton: +1 / Neutron: 0 / Electron: -1
title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

front: Why is chlorine's relative atomic mass 35.5, not a whole number?
answer: It is a weighted average of its two isotopes, chlorine-35 (75%) and chlorine-37 (25%), which isn't a whole number.
title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

front: Why do elements in the same group of the periodic table react in similar ways?
answer: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which controls how an element reacts.
title: Atoms, Elements, Compounds and the Model of the Atom

front: What are the four main factors that increase the rate of a reaction?
answer: Temperature / Concentration (or pressure for gases) / Surface area / Catalysts
title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

front: Why does increasing the pressure of a gaseous reaction increase its rate?
answer: It forces the gas particles closer together, so they collide more often.
title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

front: Why does the total volume of gas produced stay the same at different acid concentrations, even though the rate changes?
answer: The same mass of marble chips is used each time, so the same amount of gas forms - just faster or slower.
title: Rates of Reaction and Collision Theory

front: A homeostatic control system has three essential components. What are they?
answer: Receptors / Coordination centres / Effectors
title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System

front: What are the three types of neurone in the nervous pathway?
answer: Sensory neurones / Relay neurones / Motor neurones
title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System

front: Why are reflex actions faster than a voluntary response?
answer: They are coordinated by the spinal cord or an unconscious part of the brain, bypassing the slower conscious-thought pathway.
title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System

front: What are the five contact forces?
answer: Friction / Air resistance / Tension / Normal contact force / Upthrust
title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces

front: What are the three non-contact forces?
answer: Gravitational force / Electrostatic force / Magnetic force
title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces

front: Why do your hands warm up when you rub them together?
answer: Friction between your hands converts kinetic energy into thermal energy.
title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces

front: Why do you weigh less on the Moon even though your mass is unchanged?
answer: The Moon's gravitational field strength is much weaker than Earth's, and weight depends on field strength, not just mass.
title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces

front: What are the six Group 1 elements (the alkali metals)?
answer: Lithium (Li) / Sodium (Na) / Potassium (K) / Rubidium (Rb) / Caesium (Cs) / Francium (Fr)
title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

front: What are the five Group 7 elements (the halogens)?
answer: Fluorine (F) / Chlorine (Cl) / Bromine (Br) / Iodine (I) / Astatine (At)
title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

front: Why does reactivity increase going down Group 1?
answer: The outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is lost more easily.
title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

front: Why does reactivity decrease going down Group 7?
answer: The outer shell is further from the nucleus, so the attraction for an incoming electron is weaker.
title: The Periodic Table and Its Groups

front: What are the three stages of the cell cycle?
answer: Growth and DNA replication / Mitosis (nucleus divides) / Division (cytoplasm and membrane split)
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: What are the three main sources of stem cells?
answer: Embryonic stem cells / Adult stem cells / Meristem tissue in plants
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Why does DNA replicate before a cell undergoes mitosis?
answer: So that when the cell divides, each of the two daughter cells gets a complete, identical copy of the chromosomes.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Why can plant root hair cells absorb mineral ions even from very dilute soil water?
answer: Active transport uses energy from respiration to move the ions against their concentration gradient, from low to high concentration.
title: Cell Division and Transport

front: Why does the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring quadruple when the extension doubles?
answer: Elastic potential energy depends on extension squared, so doubling the extension multiplies the energy by 2 squared, which is 4.
title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law

front: Why is the energy transferred during inelastic deformation not fully recoverable?
answer: Some of the energy is dissipated as heat rather than being stored for release.
title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law

front: What are the six main endocrine glands in the body?
answer: Pituitary gland / Thyroid gland / Adrenal glands / Pancreas / Ovaries / Testes
title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

front: Type 2 diabetes has five known risk factors. What are they?
items: Unhealthy diet high in sugar and fat
answer: Obesity / Sedentary lifestyle / Unhealthy diet high in sugar and fat / Family history / Ethnicity
title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

front: Why is adrenaline release controlled by the nervous system rather than by negative feedback?
answer: It needs to be a rapid, short-term response, which is what nervous control provides rather than slower hormonal feedback.
title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

front: Why does blood glucose stay high in a person with Type 1 diabetes after a meal?
answer: No insulin is produced, so glucose cannot be taken up by cells or stored as glycogen by the liver.
title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control

front: What are the three fossil fuels?
answer: Coal / Oil / Natural gas
title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

front: Which six energy resources are renewable?
answer: Wind / Solar / Hydroelectric / Tidal / Geothermal / Biomass
title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

front: Why do fossil fuel and nuclear power stations supply the base load rather than wind or solar?
answer: They provide a constant, reliable supply, while wind and solar output depends on the weather and can't be guaranteed.
title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

front: Why does lubricating moving parts in a machine reduce wasted energy?
answer: It reduces friction between the parts, so less energy is wasted as heat.
title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources

front: What three conditions does the Haber process use to balance yield and rate?
answer: Compromise temperature (about 450°C) / High pressure (about 200 atm) / Iron catalyst
title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium

front: Le Châtelier's principle predicts equilibrium shifts from changes in three conditions. What are they?
answer: Temperature / Pressure (for gaseous reactions) / Concentration
title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium

front: Why doesn't adding a catalyst change the position of equilibrium?
answer: It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster.
title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium

front: Why doesn't the copper sulfate colour-change test prove that water is pure?
answer: It only shows that water is present; you'd need to check the boiling point (100°C) to confirm purity.
title: Reversible Reactions and Equilibrium

front: Four hormones control the menstrual cycle. What are they?
answer: FSH / LH / Oestrogen / Progesterone
title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception

front: What are the four stages of the menstrual cycle, in order?
answer: Menstruation (days 1-4) / Repair and build-up (days 4-14) / Ovulation (day 14) / Maintenance (days 14-28)
title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception

front: Why does a surge in LH happen around day 14 of the cycle?
answer: Rising oestrogen from the maturing follicle stimulates the pituitary gland to release a surge of LH.
title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception

front: Why does the menstrual cycle restart when progesterone levels fall?
answer: Progesterone no longer inhibits FSH, so FSH production resumes and starts the cycle again.
title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception

front: What four things make up the circuit used to investigate a component's I-V characteristics?
answer: Variable power supply / Ammeter in series / Voltmeter in parallel / The component being tested
title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference

front: Why does a thermistor's resistance decrease as it heats up?
answer: The semiconductor material releases more charge carriers as it heats up, making it easier for current to flow.
title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference

front: Why does an LDR's resistance decrease in brighter light?
answer: Photons of light release more charge carriers in the semiconductor, making it easier for current to flow.
title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference

front: What are the first four alkanes, from smallest to largest?
answer: Methane (CH4) / Ethane (C2H6) / Propane (C3H8) / Butane (C4H10)
title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking

front: Fractional distillation separates crude oil into six fractions. What are they, from top to bottom of the column?
answer: Gases (LPG) / Petrol / Kerosene (jet fuel) / Diesel / Fuel oil / Bitumen
title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking

front: Why does incomplete combustion produce carbon monoxide instead of carbon dioxide?
answer: There isn't enough oxygen present for the hydrocarbon to burn completely into carbon dioxide.
title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking

front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous to breathe in?
answer: It binds to haemoglobin in the blood, preventing the blood from transporting oxygen.
title: Crude Oil, Hydrocarbons and Cracking

front: The digestive system uses three main groups of enzymes. What are they?
answer: Amylase / Protease / Lipase
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: After digestion, food is broken down into three types of product ready to be absorbed. What are they?
answer: Simple sugars (glucose) / Amino acids / Glycerol and fatty acids
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why does emulsifying fat into smaller droplets speed up fat digestion?
answer: It increases the fat's surface area, so more lipase molecules can bind to it and break it down at the same time.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why must large food molecules be digested before the body can use them?
answer: Large, insoluble food molecules must be broken into small, soluble molecules so they can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
title: Organisation and the Digestive System

front: Why does an object's velocity change when it reverses direction, even if its speed stays the same?
answer: Velocity includes direction as well as speed, so a change in direction changes the velocity even when the speed is unchanged.
title: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration

front: What are the three main types of chemical bonding?
answer: Ionic bonding (transferring electrons) / Covalent bonding (sharing electrons) / Metallic bonding (sharing delocalised electrons)
title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding

front: How can you tell which of the three bonding types a substance has, from its elements?
answer: Metal + non-metal -> ionic / Non-metal + non-metal -> covalent / Metal + metal -> metallic
title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding

front: Why is nitrogen gas (N2) very stable and unreactive?
answer: Its two atoms are joined by a strong triple covalent bond, sharing three pairs of electrons.
title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding

front: Why does magnesium form a 2+ ion rather than a 1+ ion?
answer: Magnesium has two electrons in its outer shell, and it must lose both to get a full outer shell.
title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding

front: What four criteria must be met for two forces to be a Newton's third law pair?
answer: Same type of force / Equal in size / Opposite in direction / Act on two different objects
title: Newton's Laws of Motion

front: Why does a full shopping trolley accelerate less than an empty one when pushed with the same force?
answer: The full trolley has more mass, and for the same force, greater mass produces less acceleration.
title: Newton's Laws of Motion

front: Why does a rocket accelerate upwards when it pushes exhaust gases downwards?
answer: By Newton's third law, the gases push back on the rocket with an equal and opposite force, propelling it upwards.
title: Newton's Laws of Motion

front: What are the four main types of structure in chemistry?
answer: Giant ionic / Simple covalent (small molecules) / Giant covalent / Giant metallic
title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes

front: Carbon has four allotropes. What are they?
answer: Diamond / Graphite / Graphene / Fullerenes
title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes

front: Why do giant covalent structures have very high melting and boiling points?
answer: A large number of strong covalent bonds must be broken, which takes a lot of energy.
title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes

front: When a simple covalent substance melts, why do the atoms inside each molecule stay joined together?
answer: Only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules break; the strong covalent bonds within each molecule stay intact.
title: Structure, Properties and Carbon Allotropes

front: A paint formulation has four main components. What are they?
answer: Pigment (colour) / Solvent (keeps it liquid) / Binder (makes it stick) / Additives (control drying/finish)
title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

front: What are the five steps of the paper chromatography method?
items: Draw a pencil line near the bottom
Add spots of each substance on the line
Pour a shallow layer of solvent in
Lower the paper into the solvent to run
Remove before the solvent reaches the top
answer: Draw a pencil line near the bottom / Add spots of each substance on the line / Pour a shallow layer of solvent in / Lower the paper into the solvent to run / Remove before the solvent reaches the top
title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

front: Why must the solvent level stay below the pencil line in paper chromatography?
answer: If the solvent covers the spots, the substances would dissolve straight into it rather than travel up the paper.
title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

front: Why must the amount of active ingredient in a medicine tablet be carefully controlled?
answer: Too much of the active ingredient could be dangerous to the person taking it.
title: Chemical Analysis: Purity, Chromatography and Gas Tests

front: What are the four benefits of studying the human genome?
answer: Identifying genes linked to disease / Developing targeted medicines / Understanding evolutionary relationships / Advancing forensic science
title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA

front: DNA contains four bases. What are they?
answer: Adenine (A) / Thymine (T) / Cytosine (C) / Guanine (G)
title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA

front: Why does the random line-up of chromosome pairs during meiosis create genetic variation?
answer: Each gamete ends up with a different, random combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA

front: Why can DNA replicate accurately?
answer: Complementary base pairing means each strand can act as a template to build an exact new matching strand.
title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA

front: Why is the total resistance of resistors in parallel always less than the smallest individual resistor?
answer: Each extra branch gives current an additional path to flow through, so more current flows overall for the same voltage.
title: Series and Parallel Circuits

front: Why is the current the same at every point in a series circuit?
answer: There's only one path for charge to flow, so every charge leaving the cell must pass through each component in turn.
title: Series and Parallel Circuits

front: What are the three types of blood vessel in the body?
answer: Arteries / Veins / Capillaries
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Blood has four main components. What are they?
answer: Plasma / Red blood cells / White blood cells / Platelets
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Why is a double circulatory system more efficient than a single one?
answer: Blood is pumped a second time after returning from the lungs, keeping it at high pressure so organs get oxygen fast enough for respiration.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: Why are red blood cells biconcave in shape?
answer: The biconcave shape gives a larger surface area to volume ratio, allowing more efficient oxygen absorption.
title: The Heart, Blood and Circulatory Disease

front: What are the five key plant tissues?
answer: Epidermal tissue / Palisade mesophyll / Spongy mesophyll / Xylem / Phloem
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Which four environmental factors increase the rate of transpiration?
answer: Higher temperature / Lower humidity / More air movement (wind) / Higher light intensity
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Why does lower humidity increase the rate of transpiration?
answer: Lower humidity creates a steeper concentration gradient between the leaf and the air, so water diffuses out of the leaf faster.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: Why does windy weather increase the rate of transpiration?
answer: Wind carries away water vapour from the leaf surface, keeping a steep diffusion gradient that pulls more water out.
title: Health, Non-Communicable Diseases and Plant Tissues

front: A gene has three possible genotype combinations. What are they?
answer: BB - homozygous dominant / Bb - heterozygous / bb - homozygous recessive
title: Genetic Inheritance and Inherited Disorders

front: Why can't polydactyly be carried without symptoms, unlike cystic fibrosis?
answer: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele, so a single copy is always enough to cause the condition.
title: Genetic Inheritance and Inherited Disorders

front: What are the four steps for calculating a reacting mass from a balanced equation?
items: Calculate moles of the known substance
Use the ratio for the unknown
answer: Write the balanced equation / Calculate moles of the known substance / Use the ratio for the unknown / Convert moles back to mass
title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations

front: Why does adding more of the excess reactant make no difference to the amount of product formed?
answer: The reaction stops once the limiting reactant runs out, however much of the other reactant is left over.
title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations

front: Why does a higher concentration of a solution lead to a faster reaction rate?
answer: There are more solute particles per unit volume, causing more frequent collisions between reactant particles.
title: Quantitative Chemistry: Mass, Moles and Concentrations

front: What were the three main processes that removed carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere?
answer: Photosynthesis / Dissolving in the oceans / Formation of fossil fuels
title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect

front: What are the four main human activities that have raised atmospheric carbon dioxide since the Industrial Revolution?
answer: Burning fossil fuels / Deforestation / Agriculture / Landfill
title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect

front: Why does reducing carbon footprints require international cooperation?
answer: Climate change is a global issue, so action by just one country alone has only limited effect.
title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect

front: Why can rising temperatures amplify the greenhouse effect through water vapour?
answer: As temperatures rise, more water evaporates into the air, and water vapour is itself a greenhouse gas.
title: The Earth's Atmosphere and Greenhouse Effect

front: What are the three common fuse ratings used in UK plugs?
title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid

front: Why does increasing the transmission voltage reduce the current flowing in the National Grid's cables?
answer: Power equals voltage times current, and power stays roughly constant, so increasing the voltage means the current must fall.
title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid

front: Why are circuit breakers generally considered safer than fuses?
answer: They react faster than fuses to a current surge, cutting off the circuit more quickly.
title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid

front: What are the four factors that increase a driver's thinking distance?
answer: Tiredness / Alcohol and drugs / Distractions / Speed
title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum

front: What are three safety features that reduce injury by increasing collision time?
answer: Crumple zones / Seat belts / Airbags
title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum

front: Why does worn tyre tread reduce a car's grip on the road?
answer: Tread grooves channel water away from the tyre; when worn, less water is cleared, so the tyre grips less well.
title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum

front: Why do the fragments of an explosion move apart with equal and opposite momenta?
answer: The total momentum before the explosion is zero, so by conservation of momentum, the total afterwards must also be zero.
title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum

front: What are the four types of pathogen?
answer: Bacteria / Viruses / Fungi / Protists
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: White blood cells defend the body in three main ways. What are they?
answer: Phagocytosis / Antibody production / Antitoxin production
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Why does Tobacco Mosaic Virus stunt an infected plant's growth?
answer: The mosaic pattern of discolouration it causes reduces the leaf's ability to photosynthesise, which stunts growth.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: Why is phagocytosis called a non-specific defence?
answer: Phagocytes engulf and digest any pathogen they meet, rather than targeting one particular type.
title: Communicable Diseases and Human Defences

front: What are four examples of transverse waves?
answer: Light (and other EM waves) / Radio waves / Water surface ripples / S-waves (earthquakes)
title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour

front: What are the six steps of the ripple tank required practical?
items: Set up the tank with a motor-driven dipper
Switch on the lamp above the tank
Adjust the dipper frequency and observe the pattern
Measure the distance across several wavelengths
Count waves passing a fixed point over time
Calculate wave speed using v = fλ
answer: Set up the tank with a motor-driven dipper / Switch on the lamp above the tank / Adjust the dipper frequency and observe the pattern / Measure the distance across several wavelengths / Count waves passing a fixed point over time / Calculate wave speed using v = fλ
title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour

front: Why must the water depth be kept constant across a ripple tank?
answer: Changing the water depth changes the wave speed, which would make results inconsistent.
title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour

front: Why does measuring across several wavelengths give a more accurate value than measuring just one?
answer: Spreading any measurement error over many wavelengths reduces its effect on the result, lowering the percentage error.
title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour

front: Fossils can form in three main ways. What are they?
items: Preservation in special conditions (ice, peat, amber)
answer: Mineralisation (hard parts replaced by minerals) / Casts and impressions (e.g. footprints) / Preservation in special conditions (ice, peat, amber)
title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection

front: What are the four steps by which a bacterial population becomes antibiotic resistant?
answer: Random mutation gives resistance / Antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria / Resistant bacterium reproduces / Whole population becomes resistant
title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection

front: Why are rare beneficial mutations described as the driving force behind evolution?
answer: They give an organism a survival advantage, so natural selection favours that trait and it becomes more common over generations.
title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection

front: Why did Darwin's Galápagos finches have different beak shapes on different islands?
answer: Each beak shape was suited to a different food source available on that island.
title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection

front: What are the six changes of state?
answer: Melting / Boiling / Evaporation / Condensation / Freezing / Sublimation
title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State

front: Why does evaporation cause a liquid to cool down?
answer: Only the fastest, most energetic particles escape, so the average energy - and therefore the temperature - of the liquid left behind falls.
title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State

front: Why are solids generally the densest state of matter and gases the least dense?
answer: In solids, the particles are packed closely together; in gases, they are spread far apart.
title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State

front: What are the four atmospheric pollutants produced by burning fuels?
answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) / Sulfur dioxide (SO2) / Nitrogen oxides (NOx) / Particulates
title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects

front: What are three effects of acid rain?
items: Damages trees and leaches minerals from soil
Lowers lake and river pH, killing aquatic life
answer: Corrodes limestone and marble buildings / Damages trees and leaches minerals from soil / Lowers lake and river pH, killing aquatic life
title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects
problems: the set is not closed in the lesson

front: Why are catalytic converters useful for reducing both carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxide pollution?
answer: They convert both pollutants at once into less harmful gases: carbon dioxide and nitrogen.
title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects

front: Why does flue gas desulfurisation reduce a power station's contribution to acid rain?
answer: It removes sulfur dioxide from the waste gases before they leave the chimney, so less reaches the atmosphere.
title: Atmospheric Pollutants and Their Effects

front: Why can the thermite reaction be used to weld railway tracks?
answer: The reaction is so exothermic that it produces molten iron, which can fuse the rails together.
title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction

front: Why do more reactive metals lose electrons more easily than less reactive metals?
answer: Their outer electrons are further from the nucleus, so they are removed more easily.
title: Reactivity of Metals and Metal Extraction

front: A heating curve has five regions. What are they, in order?
answer: Solid heating (temp rises) / Melting (temp constant) / Liquid heating (temp rises) / Boiling (temp constant) / Gas heating (temp rises)
title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

front: What are the four steps needed to calculate the total energy to heat ice into steam?
answer: Heat the ice to 0°C / Melt the ice at 0°C / Heat the water to 100°C / Boil the water at 100°C
title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

front: Why does insulating the block improve the accuracy of a specific heat capacity experiment?
answer: It reduces the thermal energy lost to the surroundings, so more of the supplied energy goes into heating the block.
title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat

front: What are the three domains in Woese's classification system?
answer: Archaea / Bacteria / Eukarya
title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology

front: Adaptations that help organisms survive come in three types. What are they?
answer: Structural adaptations / Behavioural adaptations / Functional adaptations
title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology

front: Why did the three-domain system replace the five-kingdom model of classification?
answer: Advances in biochemistry and genome analysis showed the five-kingdom system was too simple to reflect real evolutionary relationships.
title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology

front: Why do cacti have spines instead of leaves?
answer: Having spines instead of leaves reduces the amount of water the cactus loses through transpiration.
title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology

front: What are the four stages of a life cycle assessment?
answer: Extracting raw materials / Manufacturing and processing / Use and distribution / Disposal
title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability

front: What are the three Rs for reducing the environmental impact of products?
answer: Reduce / Reuse / Recycle
title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability

front: Why are phytomining and bioleaching more environmentally friendly than traditional mining, even though they're slower?
answer: They don't need huge amounts of energy and don't produce large volumes of waste rock.
title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability

front: Why must waste water be treated before it's released into the environment?
answer: Untreated waste water would pollute rivers and seas and could spread disease.
title: Using Earth's Resources and Sustainability

front: What three measures help reduce the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria?
answer: Don't prescribe antibiotics inappropriately / Patients complete the full course / Restrict agricultural use of antibiotics
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: A new drug must be tested for three things before it reaches patients. What are they?
answer: Toxicity (is it safe?) / Efficacy (does it work?) / Dose (the right amount)
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why does herd immunity protect people who cannot be vaccinated themselves?
answer: With enough of the population immune, the pathogen can't find enough hosts to spread to those who aren't protected.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: Why is a new drug tested on live animals during preclinical testing?
answer: To see how it behaves in a whole living organism and rule out drugs too dangerous to trial on humans.
title: Vaccination, Antibiotics and Drug Development

front: What are the six steps for making a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt?
items: Add base until it's in excess
Heat the filtrate until crystals form
answer: Warm the acid gently / Add base until it's in excess / Filter to remove excess solid / Heat the filtrate until crystals form / Cool and let crystals form / Pat the crystals dry
title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

front: What are the three ways to measure the pH of a solution?
answer: Litmus paper (simple acid/alkali test) / Universal indicator (colour for every pH) / pH meter (most precise reading)
title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

front: Why can a weak acid still be described as weak even when it is concentrated?
answer: Concentration measures how much acid is dissolved; strength measures how much of it ionises - the two are independent.
title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

front: Why does the pH rise towards 7 during neutralisation?
answer: H+ ions from the acid react with OH- ions from the alkali to form water, leaving fewer free H+ ions.
title: Reactions of Acids, pH and Neutralisation

front: Which three types of electromagnetic radiation are ionising?
answer: Ultraviolet (UV) / X-rays / Gamma rays
title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum

front: Why are gamma rays more dangerous than radio waves?
answer: Gamma rays have a much higher frequency, and higher frequency means the wave carries more energy.
title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum

front: Why do radiographers stand behind lead-lined screens when taking X-ray images?
answer: X-rays are ionising and can damage cells, so lead shielding protects them from repeated exposure.
title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum

front: What are the three main types of nuclear radiation emitted by unstable nuclei?
answer: Alpha (α) / Beta (β) / Gamma (γ)
title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life

front: Why is contamination generally more dangerous than irradiation?
answer: With contamination, radioactive material stays on or inside you, so you can't move away from it and exposure continues.
title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life

front: Why doesn't gamma emission change a nucleus's mass number or atomic number?
answer: Gamma radiation is an electromagnetic wave with no mass and no charge, so nothing is lost from the nucleus.
title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life

front: What are the three main factors affecting the rate of photosynthesis?
answer: Light intensity / Carbon dioxide concentration / Temperature
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Plants use the glucose made by photosynthesis for five main purposes. What are they?
answer: Respiration (release energy) / Storage as starch / Storage as fats and oils / Making cellulose / Making amino acids and proteins
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: On a bright, sunny day, why might carbon dioxide be the limiting factor for photosynthesis?
answer: There is already plenty of light, but not enough carbon dioxide for the plant to photosynthesise any faster.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

front: Why does anaerobic respiration transfer less energy than aerobic respiration?
answer: The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so much less energy is released than in aerobic respiration.
title: Photosynthesis and Respiration

More reactive than hydrogen -> hydrogen produced
Halide ions present -> halogen at anode
No halide ions -> oxygen at anode
answer: Less reactive than hydrogen -> metal deposited / More reactive than hydrogen -> hydrogen produced / Halide ions present -> halogen at anode / No halide ions -> oxygen at anode

front: Why is aluminium recycling important?
answer: Recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from bauxite.
title: Electrolysis

front: Why does sodium hydroxide solution form during the electrolysis of brine?
answer: Hydrogen and chlorine gases are discharged from the solution, leaving the unreacted Na+ and OH- ions behind.

front: What are the four levels of ecological organisation, from smallest to largest?
answer: Organism / Population / Community / Ecosystem
title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact

front: Carbon dioxide is returned to the atmosphere in three ways. What are they?
answer: Respiration / Combustion (burning fossil fuels or wood) / Decomposition
title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact

front: Why does eutrophication kill aquatic organisms?
answer: Fertiliser runoff causes algal blooms that block light and use up oxygen in the water, suffocating aquatic life.
title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact

front: Why did the introduction of grey squirrels cause a decline in red squirrels in the UK?
answer: Grey squirrels outcompete red squirrels for food and carry a disease, squirrel pox, that harms reds.
title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact

front: Which four materials are magnetic?
answer: Iron / Steel / Nickel / Cobalt
title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect

front: What are three ways to make an electromagnet stronger?
answer: Increase the current / Add more turns of wire / Use a softer iron core
title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect

front: Why is an induced magnet always attracted to the permanent magnet that induces it, never repelled?
answer: Its nearest pole always lines up opposite to the permanent magnet's pole, so the poles always attract.
title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect

front: Why would a simple motor's coil stop turning after half a turn without a commutator?
answer: Without reversing the current, the forces on the coil would push it back the other way instead of continuing round.

front: What are four everyday examples of exothermic reactions?
answer: Combustion (burning fuels) / Neutralisation / Oxidation (e.g. rusting, respiration) / Hand warmers
title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions

front: What are four everyday examples of endothermic reactions?
answer: Thermal decomposition / Citric acid + sodium hydrogen carbonate / Sports cold packs / Photosynthesis
title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions

front: Why do endothermic reactions still need an activation energy hill, even though they take in energy overall?
answer: Every reaction, exothermic or endothermic, needs an initial energy input to get started, whatever its overall energy change.
title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions

front: Why does a catalyst leave the reactant and product energy levels unchanged on a reaction profile?
answer: A catalyst only provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; it doesn't change the reactants' or products' energy.
title: Energy Changes in Chemical Reactions
